common_name: Reward Orchid Cactus (Rich Red Epicactus)

planting.note: Root a callused stem-segment cutting in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark or cactus mix in bright indirect light; Reward, like most named epicactus hybrids, blooms best when kept slightly pot-bound.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix and place in bright indirect light, shielding the flattened, strap-like stems from harsh midday sun. Reward is a long-established named epiphyllum hybrid prized for its richly saturated red flowers, which open wide for a day or two during the late spring and summer bloom season. As with other epicactus hybrids descended from jungle cactus species such as Epiphyllum and Disocactus, it appreciates regular moisture and light feeding while actively growing and budding, followed by a slightly drier rest in winter. Move plants to a frost-free location before cold weather arrives, since it is reliably hardy outdoors only in zone 10-11.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Discovery Orchid Cactus (Large White-Flowered Epicactus)

planting.note: Root a callused stem-segment cutting in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark or cactus mix in bright indirect light; give Discovery a slightly crowded pot to encourage reliable budding.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, keeping the flattened, arching stems out of direct midday sun. Discovery is a classic named epiphyllum hybrid grown for its large, creamy-white flowers, which open widely for a night and a following day with a light fragrance typical of many epicactus hybrids. It descends from jungle cactus species such as Epiphyllum and Disocactus and wants regular moisture and light bloom-boosting fertilizer through the growing season, with a cooler, drier rest in winter. Bring plants indoors or under cover before frost, since it is reliably hardy outdoors only in zone 10-11.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Broadleaf Rhipsalis (Elliptic Mistletoe Cactus)

planting.note: Root a several-inch stem-segment cutting, callused for a couple of days, in a light, well-drained epiphytic mix of bark, perlite, and potting soil kept in bright, indirect light.

directions: Pot in a light, fast-draining mix of bark, perlite, and potting soil, and hang or display in bright, indirect light away from direct sun that can bleach the flattened, paddle-like stem segments. Rhipsalis elliptica forms cascading chains of broad, elliptical, jointed pads and is grown chiefly as a foliage houseplant, though mature specimens can produce small pale flowers followed by translucent berries. As an epiphyte from humid forest habitats it prefers consistent moisture and higher humidity in active growth, with a modest dry-down between waterings, and resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Keep it frost-free and out of cold drafts, since it is a tender tropical houseplant outside of zone 10-11.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Houlletia Rhipsalis (Toothed-Leaf Mistletoe Cactus)

planting.note: Root a several-inch stem-segment cutting, callused for a couple of days, in a light, well-drained epiphytic mix of bark, perlite, and potting soil kept in bright, indirect light.

directions: Grow in a light, fast-draining mix of bark, perlite, and potting soil, and display in a hanging basket in bright, indirect light. Rhipsalis houlletiana is distinguished from its relatives by flattened, jointed stem segments with gently scalloped or notched margins, and it produces small pinkish-white flowers with prominent red anthers followed by pale berries. Native to humid Brazilian forest understories as an epiphyte, it wants consistently moist but never soggy roots and appreciates higher humidity, misting, or a pebble tray during active growth. Protect from frost and cold drafts year-round, since it is reliably hardy outdoors only in zone 10-11 and is otherwise grown as a houseplant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Gladstoniana Water Lily (Giant Hardy White Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the tuberous rootstock horizontally in a large aquatic basket of heavy clay loam capped with pea gravel, then lower the crown 12 to 24 inches beneath the water surface in full sun once the water has begun to warm in spring.

directions: Gladstoniana is one of the largest-flowered hardy white water lilies grown, producing enormous, cup-shaped, pure white blooms with a boss of golden stamens held just above sprawling, deep-green pads. It is an extremely vigorous grower, so it needs a sizable pond or a very large planting container to avoid overwhelming smaller neighbors, and it rewards the extra room with a heavy, reliable bloom flush through summer. Feed with aquatic fertilizer tablets monthly during the growing season and divide the crowded rootstock every few years to maintain vigor and flower size. In regions where ponds freeze solid, sink the container below the ice line so the dormant crown survives winter.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: William Falconer Water Lily (Classic Hardy Blackish-Red Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the rootstock horizontally in a wide basket of heavy garden loam topped with gravel and submerge so the crown sits 8 to 18 inches below the surface in a calm, sunny part of the pond.

directions: Introduced at the turn of the twentieth century and named for the noted American horticulturist William Falconer, this cultivar remains one of the darkest hardy water lilies available, opening deep blackish-crimson and deepening further as the bloom ages against young foliage flushed with maroon. It is a moderate grower, better suited to mid-sized ponds than the largest Marliac-type whites, and blooms freely from early to late summer. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bud production, feed monthly with aquatic tablets, and divide the crown every three to four years once flowering declines from overcrowding.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Perry's Pink Water Lily (Free-Flowering Hardy Pink Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the tuber horizontally in a basket of heavy aquatic soil topped with gravel and lower it 8 to 18 inches below the water's surface in a sunny, sheltered spot as the pond warms in spring.

directions: Bred by pioneering water gardener Perry D. Slocum, this cultivar bears medium-sized, star-shaped, clear pink flowers held just above the water and is prized for how freely and continuously it blooms through the entire warm season compared with older pink hardies. Its moderate spread makes it a good fit for mid-sized backyard ponds as well as large tubs. Feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets, remove faded flowers to keep new buds coming, and lift and divide the rootstock every few years as the crown becomes congested.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Perry's Orange Sunset Water Lily (Changeable Hardy Peach-to-Orange Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the tuberous rootstock horizontally in a wide container of heavy clay loam capped with pea gravel, then submerge so the crown sits 8 to 18 inches beneath the surface in full sun.

directions: Another Perry D. Slocum introduction, this semi-double hardy cultivar opens a soft peachy apricot and deepens toward warm orange as each flower ages, giving a two-toned effect across a mature planting when several ages of bloom are open together. It is a dependable, floriferous grower well suited to home ponds of moderate size. Feed monthly through the growing season with aquatic plant tablets, deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and divide the rootstock every three to four years to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Black Princess Water Lily (Deep Red-Black Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the rootstock horizontally in a wide aquatic basket of heavy loam topped with gravel and lower it 8 to 16 inches below the water surface in a calm, full-sun location.

directions: Black Princess produces some of the darkest blooms among hardy water lilies, opening deep garnet-red and appearing nearly black in low light or against the dark surface of a pond, held above compact, purple-flushed young foliage. Its restrained spread makes it a good choice for smaller ponds and large tub gardens where a bold, dramatic color accent is wanted without an overly vigorous spreader. Feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets, deadhead to encourage repeat bloom, and divide the crown every few years once flowering slows from overcrowding.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Peter Slocum Water Lily (Vigorous Changeable Pink Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the tuber horizontally in a large basket of heavy clay soil capped with gravel, then submerge so the crown rests 12 to 24 inches below the water's surface in full sun.

directions: Named for Peter Slocum, son of noted water lily hybridizer Perry D. Slocum, this vigorous hardy cultivar opens soft pink and deepens to a richer rose as the flower matures, producing an attractive mix of shades across a well-established planting. It is a strong, free-spreading grower best given a sizable pond rather than a small tub. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly during the growing season, deadhead spent blooms to keep new buds forming, and divide the rootstock every three to four years to maintain flowering vigor.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Robinsoniana Water Lily (Classic Changeable Copper-Orange Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the rootstock horizontally in a wide container of heavy garden loam topped with pea gravel and lower it 8 to 18 inches below the surface in a sunny, still section of the pond.

directions: Raised by the French nurseryman Latour-Marliac in the 1890s, Robinsoniana is a classic changeable hardy water lily whose flowers open apricot-orange flushed with copper-red and shift toward deeper red-orange tones as they age, set against foliage mottled with maroon. It is a moderate grower well suited to mid-sized ponds and has remained popular for well over a century for its unusual, warm coloring among mostly pink and white hardy types. Feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets, remove spent flowers, and divide the crown every three to four years as it becomes congested.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: General Pershing Water Lily (Classic Fragrant Tropical Orchid-Pink Day-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond only once the water has warmed well above 70F, since this tropical selection is cold-sensitive.

directions: Introduced around 1920 and long a favorite among water gardeners, General Pershing bears very large, fragrant, orchid-pink flowers with broad, slightly ruffled petals that open during the day on strong stems held well above the pads. It is a vigorous, reliable bloomer that has remained in cultivation for over a century thanks to its combination of flower size, fragrance, and ease of growth. Because it is a true tropical, gardeners outside its perennial range grow it as a warm-season annual or overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in damp sand; feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets and remove spent blooms through summer.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: August Koch Water Lily (Prolific Viviparous Tropical Lavender-Blue Day-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in full sun once the pond water has warmed well past last frost, since this tropical cultivar will not tolerate cold water.

directions: Introduced in the early 1920s, August Koch is a viviparous tropical day-bloomer, meaning new plantlets sprout directly from the center of older leaves and can be detached and potted up to propagate more plants without dividing the parent tuber. Its abundant, medium-sized, lavender-blue flowers open in succession over an unusually long season, making it one of the most floriferous tropical water lilies commonly grown. Feed monthly with aquatic plant tablets, remove spent blooms and yellowing pads, and either overwinter the tuber indoors or treat as an annual where winters bring freezing water.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Margaret Mary Water Lily (Dwarf Viviparous Tropical Blue Container Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the small tuber in a shallow, wide container of heavy aquatic soil in full sun once the water is reliably warm; Margaret Mary stays compact enough to thrive in a half-barrel or glazed bowl.

directions: Margaret Mary is a diminutive, free-blooming viviparous tropical water lily that produces an abundance of small, star-shaped, violet-blue flowers over a compact spread of dark, mottled pads, making it one of the best choices for a small container water garden or tabletop tub rather than a full-sized pond. Like other viviparous types, small plantlets form at the leaf centers and can be removed and grown on to increase stock quickly. Feed sparingly with a diluted aquatic fertilizer to avoid overwhelming its small root system, and bring the tuber indoors to a warm, frost-free spot for winter where it cannot survive outdoors year-round.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: H.C. Haarstick Water Lily (Fragrant Tropical Wine-Red Night-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in full sun once the water has warmed well above 70F; site where evening blooms can be enjoyed after dusk.

directions: Bred by George Pring at the Missouri Botanical Garden in the 1920s, H.C. Haarstick is a classic tropical night-blooming water lily bearing very large, fragrant, deep wine-red flowers that open in late afternoon and remain open into the following morning. Its bold color and size have kept it in cultivation for a century as one of the standard red night-bloomers offered by specialty water garden nurseries. Because it needs consistently warm water, gardeners outside its hardy range grow it as a warm-season annual or overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in damp sand; feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets and deadhead spent flowers to sustain bloom.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Green Smoke Water Lily (Unusual Color-Changing Tropical Blue-Green Day-Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in full sun once the water has warmed well past last frost, since this tropical selection will not tolerate cold water.

directions: Green Smoke is a long-cultivated tropical day-blooming water lily prized for its unusual, ever-shifting color: buds open pale yellow-green flushed with blue at the petal tips, then shift through soft chartreuse and smoky blue-green tones as each flower ages over several days. The petals surround a contrasting deep blue-violet center, giving the flower an almost iridescent look rarely seen in other cultivars. Feed monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets, remove faded blooms and yellowing pads, and either treat as a warm-season annual or overwinter the dormant tuber indoors in damp sand where winters bring freezing water.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Turgid Haworthia (Swollen-Leaf Window Haworthia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; this species tightens and reddens under stronger light but rots quickly if kept damp.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix. Turgid haworthia forms a small, tight rosette of thick, swollen, blue-green leaves that taper to translucent, window-like tips, the whole rosette drawing inward and blushing reddish-bronze under strong light or during dry stress. Native to the Worcester-Robertson Karoo of South Africa's Western Cape, it grows wedged among quartz gravel and rock crevices, its low profile and pale windowed tips helping it blend into its stony habitat while admitting light to the leaf interior. Water only when the soil is completely dry, provide bright but indirect light to keep the compact form, and separate basal offsets once rooted to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Black Haworthia (Dark Wart Haworthia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; strong light deepens the near-black leaf color but too much direct sun can scorch it.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix. Black haworthia forms a low, spreading rosette of dark olive-green to nearly black-purple, triangular leaves whose surfaces are covered in small, raised, dull tubercles, giving the plant a somber, almost charcoal coloring unlike the pale-striped look of zebra-type relatives. Native to the Little Karoo of South Africa, it spreads by stolons to form a loose colony rather than a tight clump, and its dusky coloring intensifies with bright light and the stress of a dry season. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light to develop the deepest color without scorching, and separate rooted offsets from the spreading stolons to propagate.

common_name: Koelmans' Haworthia (Long-Stalk Window Haworthia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; this collector's species is slow to offset and best left undisturbed between repottings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix. This rare South African species forms a small clustering rosette of pointed, gray-green leaves and is best known among collectors for its unusually thick, woody flower stalk, which persists year after year and slowly branches, unlike the thin, disposable stems most haworthias send up for a single bloom. Native to rocky quartzite outcrops in Limpopo province and now protected in habitat, it is a slow grower best suited to specialist collections and shallow pots where its odd, persistent peduncle can be left in place rather than trimmed away after flowering. Water only when the soil is completely dry, provide bright but indirect light, and be patient, since offsets form slowly at the base.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: BeeDance Painted Red Bidens (Semi-Double Bicolor Trailing Apache Beggarticks)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 50F; this mounding-trailing selection fills baskets quickly without pinching.

directions: BeeDance Painted Red is a Danziger-bred selection notable for its open-faced, semi-double flowers in warm red-orange with a bright yellow reverse and center, a bicolor break that sets it apart from the solid-gold bidens types already common in the trade. The relatively flat, single-ring flower form was bred to keep the central disc accessible to pollinators, making it a strong choice for pollinator-friendly containers and baskets. Plant in a well-drained mix in full sun and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings, since soggy soil reduces flowering more than any other factor. It is self-cleaning and branches freely into a dense mounding-trailing habit, needing only light monthly feeding to sustain bloom through the warm season.

common_name: Sunsatia Blueberry Nemesia (Fragrant Trailing Blue-Purple Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant hardened-off transplants into well-drained, fertile soil; Sunsatia Blueberry's trailing habit suits hanging baskets and mixed containers better than upright border use.

directions: Sunsatia Blueberry bears rich blue-purple flowers with a small yellow throat and the same strong sweet fragrance shared across the Proven Winners Sunsatia series, on a trailing habit better suited to hanging baskets and container edges than the upright Mango selection. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and keep moisture consistent, since the fibrous root system declines quickly if allowed to dry out repeatedly. Shear back lightly after the first flush to renew dense flowering through the cool months of spring and fall, expecting a slowdown during peak summer heat before bloom resumes as temperatures moderate.

common_name: Sayamusume Edamame Soybean

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since seedlings are sensitive to cold, wet ground; a floating row cover can help hold heat for an earlier start.

directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean-specific rhizobium if soybeans haven't grown in the bed before. Sayamusume is a Japanese edamame heirloom valued for its large, elongated, light-green beans and reliably sweet, tender flavor, carried on upright plants with pods clustered two to four per cluster. Pick pods while still bright green and fully plump for fresh edamame, or leave plants to dry down further for shelling as dry soybeans. Steam or boil harvested pods briefly in well-salted water, then pop the beans free to eat as a snack or use in salads and stir-fries.

common_name: Karikachi Edamame (Karikachi No. 3 Soybean)

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed following last frost; this Hokkaido-bred cultivar tolerates cooler summer conditions better than many edamame types, suiting short-season gardens.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in full sun, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria for improved nitrogen fixation. Karikachi No. 3 is a compact, determinate Japanese heirloom bred on the island of Hokkaido for cool, short growing seasons, setting three large, sweet-flavored beans per pod on reliably productive, disease-resistant plants. Harvest whole pods once they are plump and bright green but before the shells begin to toughen or yellow. Blanch briefly in salted water before shelling and serving as a snack or in salads and stir-fries.

common_name: Kuroshinju Black Edamame Soybean

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this black-seeded heirloom needs a full season of steady summer warmth to fill its pods.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean rhizobium if soybeans are new to the bed. Kuroshinju, meaning 'black pearl' in Japanese, is a rare heirloom edamame prized for its striking black seed coat and rich, nutty, sweeter-than-average flavor, borne two to three beans per pod on upright, 2 to 2.5 foot plants. Harvest at the green-shell stage, while pods are fully plump and still green with just a cast of black showing through, rather than waiting for the beans to dry and darken completely. Steam or boil briefly in salted water and pop the beans free of the pod for eating fresh.
